doc.summary: Load, inspect and paste tmux byte buffers through an explicit endpoint.
doc.body:
Use `load/3` for binary payloads, including NUL bytes, and `show/2` to read
them back without terminal escaping or an added newline. `list/1` returns
captured metadata in tmux's newest-first order; it never loads payloads.
`paste/3` sends a named buffer to a registered pane. Direct input is available
through `tmux_pane:send_text/2`.

Names are NUL-free binaries, distinct from payload bytes. New names retain
tmux's storage rules: 3.7+ cleans names and can reject control bytes or escape
backslashes. Use observed names from `list/1` for subsequent calls. Empty load
input is tmux's no-op; it neither creates nor clears a buffer. `delete/2`
removes a buffer explicitly. Names have no persistent object identity, and
concurrent commands can replace a buffer between calls.

All operations except `capabilities/1` perform explicit I/O. They use the
one-shot transport and preserve operational errors and ownership checks.
The [buffer guide](buffers.md) shows a complete byte round trip.

examples.code:
1> {ok, V} = tmux_version:parse(<<"tmux 3.3">>), ok.
ok
2> tmux_buffer:capabilities(V).
#{paste_sanitize => false,cleaned_names => false,
  rename_replaces => false,strict_named_target => false}

doc.body:
On 3.3/3.3a, named deletion first checks existence with a zero-output `show/3`
read because native deletion falls back to the newest buffer when a name is
absent. This check does not collect a payload or depend on the list bounds.
It is not atomic: concurrent removal after the check can trigger that fallback.
Use external serialization or tmux 3.4+ when that race is unacceptable.

Look up source-derived native command declarations and feature minimums.
doc.body:
`commands/1` and `command/2` describe the exact source profiles in `profiles/0`.
Profiles cover every release in the supported tmux 3.3a–3.8 range. They do not
contact tmux, interpret its arguments or qualify another build.
Canonical command names are lookup keys; aliases remain metadata. A native
declaration does not mean this library provides a typed facade for it. Use
`tmux_command:raw/2` for an explicit trusted command.

`describe/1` reports selected native feature minimums. `require/2` compares a
parsed version with one of those minimums; it does not perform I/O or dispatch
the command. Numeric minimum checks also accept uncatalogued and tracking
versions, preserving the distinction from exact parser discovery. They do not
establish runtime or CI qualification. Use `tmux_server:version/1` to obtain the
version captured by a registered endpoint.

The [generated reference](commands-reference.md) records source profiles and
parser declarations. Maintaining the catalogue needs a tmux source checkout;
installed consumers use compiled data and OTP only.

2> {ok, C} = tmux_capability:command(V, <<"send-keys">>), ok.

Build one tmux command without performing I/O.
doc.body:
Arguments remain binary values. Rendering protects trailing semicolons from
tmux's command separator parser. This is distinct from shell quoting and from
format expansion. A raw command is trusted application code; external services
must apply their own command allowlist and write policy.

Use `literal_format/1` only for a whole argument that tmux
expands as a format, such as a new name or cwd. It does not encode a value
nested in a format expression. tmux's stored-name escaping and session-name
substitutions still apply. Use `literal_format/2` with mode time
for commands such as display-message that also expand strftime percent
directives. This protects one format-expansion pass, not later visual style
rendering or recursive/nested expansion. No renderer reverses stored-name
semantics.

`launch/1` distinguishes executable argv from an explicitly
requested shell command. A singleton argv uses the installed helper's
exec-only mode because tmux otherwise passes one argument to its default
shell. Empty argv is invalid; default_shell explicitly requests tmux's
configured default command/shell. The internal helper uses an absolute path so
a child's cwd does not change helper resolution. Relative executable arguments
retain their native meaning.

Empty shell commands have command-specific lifetime. split-window creates a
process-free pane. new-session executes an empty shell command and can remove
the new object immediately. new-window does likewise before tmux 3.8; tmux 3.8
creates a process-free pane. Use a persistent job for parent sessions/windows
that must remain available across supported versions.

Submit commands through `tmux_server:command/3` or `tmux_operation:start/3`.
The [job guide](jobs.md) shows submission, completion and cancellation.
`tmux_session:rename_command/2` and `tmux_pane:resize_command/2` build values
bound to their row's captured origin. Execution through another endpoint
returns different_owner before native work. Construction does not validate
endpoint liveness or authorize an automatic mutation retry.

`wait_for/2` builds native channel signals, waits and advisory locks.
`source_file/2` builds configuration loading from stdin or a literal absolute
path. Both return command values without opening an endpoint or doing I/O.
`to_config/1` renders a command or bounded command list for native
configuration input, preserving argument bytes through tmux's lexer.

examples.code:
1> {ok, C} = tmux_command:raw(<<"list-panes">>, [<<"-a">>]), ok.
ok
2> tmux_command:argv(C).
[<<"list-panes">>,<<"-a">>]
3> tmux_command:literal_format(<<"api-#{pane_id}">>).
{ok,<<"api-##{pane_id}">>}
4> tmux_command:launch(#{argv => [<<"/bin/printf">>, <<"hello">>]}).
{ok,[<<"/bin/printf">>,<<"hello">>]}

doc.summary: Quote a complete literal format argument. Mode tmux protects hash expansion; mode time also protects strftime percent directives. Stored-name semantics remain tmux's own. This handles one expansion pass, not a nested operand, recursive expansion or later visual style rendering. Performs no I/O.
doc.body:
Hash runs before `[` stay unchanged because tmux preserves style-looking
prefixes for a separate drawing step. Other hashes are doubled. In time mode,
an argument containing percent bytes must fit tmux's 8191-byte strftime result
limit after hash encoding and before percent doubling; larger values return
`format_limit` with `time_bytes` and `max_bytes`. Arguments without percent
bytes skip that native time-expansion limit. The encoded 32 KiB command limit
still applies in either mode.

External services still need their own allowlists and write policy. Names are at most 128 bytes. NUL bytes are rejected, and at most 2,040 arguments fit within a 32 KiB command reservation including framing overhead.

doc.summary: Build configuration loading from stdin or one literal absolute path, without I/O. `stdin` renders `source-file -`; supply configuration bytes in the `stdin` option of `tmux_server:command/3` or `tmux_operation:start/3`. Those APIs bound input to 256 KiB including their argument reservation.
doc.body:
Paths are NUL-free POSIX byte binaries. Glob metacharacters and backslashes
are escaped so only that filename is selected; format expansion is disabled.
The combined encoded path and flags must fit `raw/2` limits. The file is read
by tmux at execution time; this builder does not open it or bound its size.

`parse_only` requests native `-n` parsing without executing the configuration's
command list. `quiet` requests native `-q` missing-file suppression; it does
not suppress syntax or execution errors. Both default to false. Configuration
is trusted tmux code, with its own variable, directive and command semantics.
Parse-only is not a sandbox. Execution can partially change server state before
an error; cancellation cannot undo those effects. Completion does not prove
that background jobs launched by the configuration have finished.

examples.code:
1> {ok, Source} = tmux_command:source_file(stdin, #{parse_only => true}), ok.
ok
2> tmux_command:argv(Source).
[<<"source-file">>,<<"-n">>,<<"--">>,<<"-">>]

                   {ok, binary()} | {error, map()}.

doc.summary: Render validated commands as native configuration text, without I/O. Accepts one command or a nonempty flat list of at most 256 commands. Returns an ASCII binary of at most 32 KiB, without a final newline. Validation uses `validate/1`; escaping growth, command count and aggregate size can return `command_limit`. Lists use native command separators between independently quoted commands. Rendering does not execute them or provide atomic execution or rollback. The text carries no origin token; executing serialized configuration requires the caller to choose and validate its destination explicitly.
doc.body:
Each argument is doublequoted. Quote, backslash, dollar, tilde, control and
non-ASCII bytes use three-digit octal escapes. Empty arguments, semicolons,
newlines and non-UTF-8 byte values remain argument data. The lexer does not
expand their variables or tilde prefixes, strip newline indentation, or
interpret them as directives, comments or additional commands.

Protection covers one lexer pass. Native command-string arguments, including
`bind-key` and `set-hook` values, can be parsed again by the receiving command.
Render each inner command string separately for its own parse boundary.

This is tmux configuration syntax, separate from `argv/1` executable arguments
and shell quoting. Native commands still interpret their values and expand
formats as usual; `literal_format/2` handles that separate boundary when
literal format values are required. Load the text explicitly with
`source_file/2`, or store it through a native command that accepts configuration
text. The [configuration guide](configuration.md) uses this renderer with
explicit execution and completion signals.

-spec wait_for(binary(), wait_action()) ->
                  {ok, t()} | {error, map()}.

doc.summary: Build a native `wait-for` command without I/O. Channels are nonempty NUL-free binary names, subject to the command reservation in `raw/2`; neither shell nor format expansion occurs. Submit through `tmux_operation:start/3` for a wait that leaves the caller free, or through `tmux_server:command/3` to await it.
doc.body:
`signal` wakes current waiters. On an unlocked channel with no waiters or
pending wakeup, it retains one wakeup for a later wait. Signaling that channel
again before a wait can clear the pending state. Signals are neither counted
nor reliably coalesced events; send once per expected wait. Channel names are
shared by all clients of the server. Use separate names for signaling and
locking. `lock` acquires an advisory channel lock or waits
for an explicit `unlock`; a completed command client's exit does not release
its acquired lock. Unlocking an unlocked channel is a native command error.

Cancellation retires the library client. It does not undo a signal or release
a lock that may already have been acquired; an uncertain lock outcome needs
application coordination before another unlock. This is not an owned mutex.

1> {ok, Signal} = tmux_command:wait_for(<<"build-ready">>, signal), ok.
ok
2> tmux_command:argv(Signal).
[<<"wait-for">>,<<"-S">>,<<"--">>,<<"build-ready">>]

Own an explicit persistent tmux control attachment.
doc.body:
`attach/3` attaches to an existing session from `m:tmux_server` and verifies
the daemon identity on that connection. The caller owns its lifetime.
Attachment changes the session's attached-client count. The command client
uses no-output and ignore-size; -E skips attachment's environment update.
The library issues no session-option writes or session-creation commands.
Configured hooks and native lifetime policies can still change state,
including on failed attach or detachment. Those effects are not rolled back.
Command submission and terminal streaming are not yet exposed.

Use `close/1` before closing the parent endpoint. Parent closing, invalidation
or caller death requests retirement, but parent close alone does not prove
this client's exit. Control close and `status/1` report its native cleanup.
Neither detachment nor cancellation reverses remote effects. Application
shutdown alone is not a verified cleanup result.

Uses attach-session with -E rather than creating a session or writing options. Configured hooks may change state; failure does not reverse their effects. The control client affects attached_count. Unexpected hook-generated reply blocks fail attachment and retire the client.
doc.body:
An attachment timeout requests cleanup. If cleanup cannot be proved within
its finite deadline, the error includes a control handle for `close/1` recovery.
The supervised owner remains until native retirement. Close explicitly to
observe cleanup, including when the parent endpoint is already closed.

Explain library exceptions through Erlang's native error formatter.
doc.body:
The shell and `erl_error:format_exception/3` call `format_error/2` through
EEP-54 stack metadata. Explanations supplement the original exception reason;
tagged results from `tmux_filter:new/2` and `tmux_select:try_where/2` retain
their existing structured data. Formatting performs no tmux I/O.

Only library-raised errors carry this metadata. Application callback failures
retain their original class, reason and stack. Coverage errors describe missing
observations; formatting never loads those observations or retries an action.
Long detail values may be abbreviated in the explanation. The exception reason
retains the original error data. See [runtime diagnostics](diagnostics.md) for
the separate, bounded Logger report contract.

doc.summary: Construct portable conditions and prepare them against captured values.
doc.body:
Local criteria use atom keys, binary text and schema-typed values. Fields and
operators conjoin. Boolean branches use 'and', 'or' and 'not'; relationships
use some/every/none/count or is/is_not. Validation examines the entire input
before evaluation. No function here performs tmux I/O. Use portable filters
with `tmux_select:where/2` or `tmux_query:where/2`; the [query
guide](querying.md) explains their different execution boundaries.

Wire version 1 uses generated camelCase field names, snake_case operators,
JSON null for known absence and {"base64": "..."} for byte operands. Byte
values never become text implicitly. Regex uses the restricted ASCII
portable_v1 dialect, absolute anchors and no flags. Preparation compiles each
pattern once. Non-ASCII subjects and exhausted match limits return errors.

Both input criteria and their normalized wire document must fit the grammar,
depth and byte limits. Resource errors can refer to the canonical wire path.

examples.code:
1> Fields = #{id => <<"%1">>, current_command => <<"vim">>}, ok.
ok
2> {ok, P} = tmux_model:pane(Fields), S = tmux_select:from_list(pane, [P]), ok.
ok
3> R = #{pattern => <<"^(vim|nvim)$">>, dialect => portable_v1}, ok.
ok
4> tmux_select:size(tmux_select:where(#{current_command => #{regex => R}}, S)).
1

dispatch are separate observations, with no atomic compare-and-act guarantee.

refresh during these actions.

`tmux_option:catalogue/1`. User options, prefixes and aliases are rejected.

raw integration remains available through `tmux_command:raw/2`. Calls perform
I/O after validation and never retry uncertain mutations. The

doc.body:
`bind/3` uses the native prefix table; `bind/4` chooses a table, repeat flag
and note. Command values use `tmux_command:to_config/1` for the stored parser
boundary. Replacing a binding resets its commands, repeat flag and note.

table through `m:tmux_option`; tmux's prefix and client table-switching rules
still apply. Registering a custom table does not select it for any client.

doc.summary: Own a command independently of an individual wait.
doc.body:
`start/3` submits a validated command through the endpoint's
bounded admission. The initiating process owns it. `await/2`
timing out abandons only that wait; `cancel/1` or owner death
retires the client and may leave an unknown tmux outcome. The endpoint
acknowledges `transfer/2` after monitoring the new owner and
before replying to the old owner. The new process does not perform a
handshake. Retired results expire after 60 seconds or earlier when the
endpoint exceeds 64 retained results or 4 MiB of retained stdout/stderr
(oldest evicted first). Closing the endpoint clears its operation results
immediately. Each operation accepts at most 16 concurrent waiters; excess
waits return too_many_waiters. `await_started/2` returns
lifecycle status once the operation leaves queued; dispatch authorization does
not establish a tmux aftereffect.

See `t:completed/0` and `t:failure/0` for
command outcomes and `t:state/0` for lifecycle status. The [job
guide](jobs.md) shows the complete workflow. Bounded OTP Logger reports
correlate outcomes by operation and endpoint generation; see
[runtime diagnostics](diagnostics.md) for levels, fields and data boundaries.

Read and change explicit tmux option tables through registered references.
doc.body:
Session, physical window and pane records from `m:tmux_model` select their
local tables. Global tables use {server, Server}, {session_defaults, Server}
or {window_defaults, Server}. Built-in canonical names and scopes are checked
against pinned source metadata; tmux otherwise lets a name override the
supplied scope flags. `m:tmux_hook` owns hook registration and execution;
hooks are rejected here. Prefixes and aliases are rejected.

`get/3` requires an explicit options map. Local-only reads are the
default; inherit = true follows tmux's table parents (pane -> window -> window
defaults, or session -> session defaults). Server options have no parent. A
missing local value or array entry returns none; an empty binary or empty
array is a value. Arrays return maps of indexes to binary values, preserving
sparse indexes. There is no hidden capture refresh or cache of option values.

Values are NUL-free binary tmux text bytes, including non-UTF-8 bytes. No
shell or format expansion is applied by this API. tmux still interprets a
built-in option according to its type: formats, shell commands and command
options may execute later when tmux uses them. This API is for trusted
application code. Numeric and flag values are canonical binary text on reads,
not Erlang numbers.

Built-in metadata covers every released version in the supported tmux
3.3a–3.8 range, including exact patch letters. Tracking and unknown versions
fail closed. User options beginning @ do not need a built-in
catalogue. The raw `tmux_command:raw/2` remains available for deliberate
newer-server integration. All mutations are one-shot I/O with observed
identity checks, not transactions. Timeouts can leave an unknown remote
outcome; mutations are never retried here. See the [scoped options
guide](options.md) for ownership and inheritance.

Create, observe and rearrange panes using registered physical IDs.
doc.body:
`split/2` accepts a pane or a window; a window means its active pane
at execution. Options (`t:split_options/0`) are direction
(horizontal or vertical), size ({cells, N} or {percent, N}), before,
full_size, zoom, cwd, env, launch and detach. It defaults to a detached
vertical split. `get/2` returns newly observed fields; existing rows
remain unchanged. Reads span several commands and do not claim atomicity.
Launch and environment options follow `tmux_session:create/2`. An absent or
zero tmux pane_pid is represented as none. A captured positive PID is an
observation, not a guarantee that the process remains alive.

A successful split followed by a failed observation retains the completed
mutation and command result in its error. `kill/1` returns the
command result. Detached or stale references cannot act. `resize_command/2`
builds a reusable value without tmux I/O; the other calls perform I/O after
validation.

`send_text/2` sends up to 2,000 literal bytes, including NUL, in one
command using tmux's hexadecimal key form. It adds no Enter key and never
splits a large input into partially applied commands. `send_keys/2`
accepts up to 256 named keys, single UTF-8 characters, {function, 1..12} and
{control, <<Letter>>}. Named keys are enter, tab, escape, backspace, space,
up, down, left, right, home, 'end', insert, delete, page_up, page_down and
back_tab. Terminal modes still govern how input is consumed; command
completion does not mean a program processed it.

`capture/2` returns stdout bytes unchanged, including final
newlines. Options (`t:capture_options/0`) are start and 'end' (line
integers or all), join_lines, escape_sequences, escape_control,
retain_trailing_spaces, alternate, pending and quiet. Defaults are tmux's
current-screen capture without escapes, joined wraps or padding. The
endpoint's output limit applies; an oversized capture returns an error.

Use `join/3`, `move/3` and `swap/3` to rearrange existing panes without
respawning their processes. `break/4` takes an explicit source window link:
breaking a window's only pane moves that membership, while breaking one of
several panes creates a new physical window. The [topology guide](panes.md)
shows the distinction. Use `get/2` or a new snapshot for updated parents and
indexes; actions leave captured values unchanged.

`pipe/3` connects a tmux-owned shell process to pane output, input or both.
It protects the shell text from tmux hash/strftime expansion; shell quoting
remains the caller's responsibility. `stop_pipe/1` closes that native pipe.
These actions do not create an Erlang output subscription or transfer process
ownership to the endpoint. Use an application acknowledgement for consumer
readiness, delivered bytes and job completion.

Build and execute explicit queries over the tmux graph.
doc.body:
Use `fetch/1` to execute a query. Constructors,
`where/2`, `limit/2`, `pushdown/2` and
`explain/1` perform no tmux I/O. Criteria are validated when added,
and repeated conditions conjoin. Fetching returns an ordered `m:tmux_select`
selection backed by a complete `m:tmux_snapshot` graph. By default the full
captured view is filtered locally. Enable native candidate exclusion with
`pushdown/2`: it can add a scan without reducing complete-graph hydration. The
candidate is a necessary condition; the full filter still runs before the limit.

Captures span commands and are not atomic. Candidate IDs excluded at one
observation cannot be recovered by later local filtering. Disabling
`pushdown/2` evaluates the complete captured view without an
earlier candidate exclusion. Numeric candidate fields come from the restricted
scalar codec and must agree with the capture's scalar observations. Text and
relationships remain local.

Captures emit bounded OTP Logger reports with their snapshot ID and endpoint
generation. See [runtime diagnostics](diagnostics.md) for observation cost,
rejection reports and configuration.

examples.code:
1> Q0 = tmux_query:panes(unopened), ok.
ok
2> Q = tmux_query:where(#{width => #{gte => 120}}, Q0), ok.
ok
3> maps:get(format, maps:get(candidate, tmux_query:explain(Q))).
<<"1">>
4> Pushed = tmux_query:pushdown(true, Q), ok.
ok
5> maps:get(format, maps:get(candidate, tmux_query:explain(Pushed))).
<<"#{e|>=|:#{pane_width},120}">>

doc.body:
Use `run/2` around a resource whose handle remains in the caller's scope.
Use `run_or_error/2` for nested scopes or fail-fast programs that need the
callback's value directly and raise when cleanup fails.
`tmux_server:with_server/2` and `tmux_server:with_owned/2` also acquire their
resources and add recovery handles when cleanup fails. This module owns no
process, timeout or retry policy; the supplied functions own those contracts.

doc.body:
Only ok proves cleanup success. Normalize resource-specific successful replies
inside the cleanup function. With successful cleanup, return {ok, Value} or
re-raise the original callback exception with its reason and stack. A callback
returning an error tuple is an ordinary value. Cleanup failure instead returns
{error, Failure} with `t:failure/0`, preserving both outcomes. An unexpected
cleanup return is recorded as invalid_cleanup_result.

an ordinary outer callback value. Keep resource handles for recovery; this
function does not infer ownership or retry cleanup.

3> Work = fun() -> error(build_failed) end, ok.
ok
4> {error, F} = tmux_scope:run(Work, fun() -> {error, busy} end), ok.
ok
5> {exception, error, build_failed, [_ | _]} = maps:get(primary, F), ok.
ok
6> maps:get(cleanup, F).
{error,busy}

control client. Each command rechecks the observed Linux process incarnation
before dispatch. Replacement between that observation and a later client
connection remains possible; same_connection requests are rejected until
persistent dispatch qualifies.

`start_owned/1` creates a separate private daemon and returns an ownership
token for `stop_owned/1`. The [ownership guide](ownership.md) explains caller
death, application shutdown and namespace cleanup.

Use `with_server/2` or `with_owned/2` for a callback scope. They attempt cleanup
after its return or exception and preserve both outcomes if cleanup fails.

The calling process owns the endpoint. `close/1` cancels queued
work, retires its one-shot clients and preserves the borrowed server. Cleanup
failure remains explicit and keeps the supervised owner alive. Successful close is
idempotent during the 60-second handle retention period. Separate
`m:tmux_control` attachments receive an invalidation notice and begin their
own retirement. Close those attachments explicitly to prove their native
cleanup. Command results preserve stdout, stderr and status; cancellation
after dispatch cannot undo
remote effects. Clients explicitly select tmux's UTF-8 mode so Unicode and the
identity probe's tab do not depend on the caller's locale. Command-specific
escaping still applies to raw command output.

Use `snapshot/1` to capture a graph for `m:tmux_snapshot` and
`m:tmux_select`. Use `m:tmux_operation` for non-blocking submission and
explicit waits; the [job guide](jobs.md) explains ownership and cleanup.

doc.body:
A window link is identified by session ID, window index and expected physical
window ID. It has no stable tmux link ID. These calls check that the observed
membership still names the expected window before dispatching an action.
Missing or replaced membership returns stale_link. A link that moves away and
back to the same coordinates and physical window cannot be distinguished.

The preflight and action use separate one-shot commands. Concurrent changes
after preflight can still affect the action; this is not atomic
compare-and-act. All input rows must belong to the same registered owner.
Re-read or explicitly bind rows when using another owner. Closed owners and
known restarts invalidate their rows. Every call performs explicit I/O after
validating its arguments.

Use `tmux_window:kill/1` to destroy a physical window across all memberships.
Use `unlink/2` to remove one membership. Existing rows and
snapshots are never refreshed by actions; use `get/3` or a
new snapshot for current memberships.
